conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you're here today because of abdominal pain. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it's that sharp, knife-like pain again—right under my sternum and in the lower left side. It feels like my old adhesions acting up. And I’ve had watery stools again, though not as bad as last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks for that. You’ve had Crohn’s disease for a while and multiple surgeries, so we know this kind of pain isn’t new. But we need to make sure nothing serious is going on this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a fever or vomiting this time, but I did throw up twice a few days ago. I haven’t eaten much—last meal was two days ago. The pain just makes it hard to want to eat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We checked your labs in the ER—your white blood cell count and kidney function are normal, and your lactate is fine. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection this time? I’ve had C. diff before—three times in the past year. I was worried it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We sent a stool test for C. difficile, and it came back negative. No salmonella or shigella either. So it doesn’t look like a new infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. But why the pain then? It’s not like my usual Crohn’s flare either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan with contrast this morning. It shows no blockage, no inflammation, and your ileorectal anastomosis looks stable. The GI team reviewed it and doesn’t think this is a Crohn’s flare—your CRP is normal, which helps rule that out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it? If it’s not Crohn’s or infection, why am I in so much pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history of multiple abdominal surgeries, adhesions are the most likely cause. Scar tissue can pull and cause sharp, localized pain like you’re describing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the pain meds I have at home aren’t helping much. Oxycodone only takes the edge off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on oral hydromorphone 2 mg every six hours as needed, plus Tylenol. We want to see if better pain control helps while we monitor you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I just reviewed your CT report again. No signs of obstruction or perforation. Everything looks stable. The GI team agrees—no need for surgery or new Crohn’s treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that, but I’m still in a lot of pain. I don’t feel like staying. I’ve been through this before, and it usually runs its course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand you’re frustrated. But leaving now means you won’t have our support if things get worse—like if you develop a blockage or dehydration. There’s even a risk of serious complications, including death.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s a risk, but I’d rather manage this at home. I know my body. I’ll use my loperamide for the diarrhea and keep taking the pain meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. If you’re certain, we’ll discharge you, but it will be against medical advice. We’ll keep your azathioprine, famotidine, and other regular meds the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m sure. I’ll follow up with my GI doctor soon. Just want to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright. We’ll prepare your discharge papers. Continue your current medications, avoid NSAIDs—they’re on your allergy list—and call us if you develop fever, vomiting, or worsening pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And I’ll keep using the hydromorphone as needed until I see my doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but only as prescribed. And please don’t drive or operate machinery while taking it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t. Thanks for explaining everything, even if I’m leaving early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. Your safety is our priority. We’ll send the discharge instructions to your primary team. Please follow up within a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re still planning to leave today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m ready to go when the paperwork is done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve documented your decision to leave against medical advice. You’re discharged now. Take care, and please reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll be careful.
